Note that p3​(s∗)≠0p_{3}(s_{*})\neq 0 or else p⁡(s,s∗)p(s;s_{*}) would be the zero solution. ∎

Finally, we consider case (III). In this case we can assume without loss of generality that

p⁡(s∗,λ)\displaystyle p(s_{*};\lambda) =(00p3​(s∗,λ)0)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&p_{3}(s_{*};\lambda)&0\end{pmatrix}
q⁡(s∗,λ)\displaystyle q(s_{*};\lambda) =(0q2​(s∗,λ)00).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&q_{2}(s_{*};\lambda)&0&0\end{pmatrix}.

In this case, the first order crossing form is a two-by-two matrix, and we need to determine its two eigenvalues. This means we must compute Q(1)​(v)Q^{(1)}(v) for v=p⁡(s∗)v=p(s_{*}) and v=q⁡(s∗)v=q(s_{*}). Since p⁡(s∗)p(s_{*}) has the same form as in Lemma 3.16, we again find that Q(1)​(p⁡(s∗))=0Q^{(1)}(p(s_{*}))=0. To compute Q(1)​(q⁡(s∗))Q^{(1)}(q(s_{*})), we modify the calculation in the proof of Lemma 3.13 to find

Q(1)​(q⁡(s∗))=⟨q⁡(s∗,λ),J​B​q​(s∗,λ)⟩=(q2​(s∗,λ))2>0.Q^{(1)}(q(s_{*}))=\langle q(s_{*},\lambda),JBq(s_{*},\lambda)\rangle=(q_{2}(s_{*};\lambda))^{2}>0.

Thus, we find that the first order crossing for is degenerate, but it is not identically zero. Thus, this case lies outside the scope of the theory developed in §2.2. Thus, we must rule it out with the following hypothesis.

Hypothesis 3.17.

The dimension of the intersection of ℓ⁡(s,0)\ell(s,0) with the sandwich plane ℓ∗s​a​n​d\ell_{*}^{sand} is at most one.

This hypothesis ensures that all crossings are simple, and of the three cases laid out after Lemma 3.15, only cases I and II are possible. Moreover should a degenerate crossing occur, the entire crossing form is identically zero, and hence the theory of §2.2 applies. We note that, in §4, we provide evidence that, for all pulses that we consider, this hypothesis is indeed satisfied.

Thus, we have proven the following monotonicity result.

Proposition 3.18.

Suppose that Hypothesis 3.17 is satisfied. For any fixed λ∈[0,λ∞]\lambda\in[0,\lambda_{\infty}], the path s↦ℓ⁡(s,λ)s\mapsto\ell(s,\lambda) as ss runs from −∞-\infty to LL has a positive contribution to the Maslov index. In other words,

Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,D2,L)=∑s∈[−∞,L]dim(ℓ⁡(s,λ)∩ℓ∗s​a​n​d)≥0.\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{2,L})=\sum_{s\in[-\infty,L]}\dim(\ell(s,\lambda)\cap\ell_{*}^{sand})\geq 0.

Finally, we prove Theorem 3.1 given at the beginning of this section.

Theorem 3.1. Suppose that Hypothesis 3.17 is satisfied. The number of positive eigenvalues of ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} is equal to the number of conjugate points in (−∞,L)(-\infty,L) counted with multiplicities.

Proof.

Via homotopy invariance and Proposition 3.9 and Proposition 3.7, we know that

Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,DL)=∑i=14Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,Di,L)=Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,D2,L)+Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,D3,L)=0.\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{L})=\sum_{i=1}^{4}\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{i,L})=\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{2,L})+\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{3,L})=0.

By the construction of the eigenvalue problem in Equation (3.7), we see that all crossings on D3,LD_{3,L} correspond to non-positive eigenvalues. Thus, if we define Mor​(ℒL)\text{Mor}(\mathcal{L}_{L}) to be the number of strictly positive eigenvalues of ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L}, then

Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,D3,L)=Mor​(ℒL)+dimker⁡ℒL.\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{3,L})=\text{Mor}(\mathcal{L}_{L})+\dim\ker\mathcal{L}_{L}.

Lastly, if there was a crossing at (0,L)(0,L), this crossing would contribute to both Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,D2,L)\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{2,L}) and Mas​(ℓ,ℓ∗s​a​n​d,D3,L)\text{Mas}(\ell,\ell_{*}^{sand};D_{3,L}). By Lemma 3.5, this can only happen if 00 is an eigenvalue of ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} and LL is a conjugate point. Therefore, the number of nonnegative eigenvalues of ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} is equal to the number of conjugate points in (−∞,L)(-\infty,L) counting multiplicity. ∎

3.2 Extension to ℝ\mathbb{R}

In general, we do not expect the spectrum of an operator on a truncated domain and an unbounded domain to be the same. In order to argue that the number of positive eigenvalues of the operator ℒ\mathcal{L} acting on (−∞,L](-\infty,L], which we called ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L}, coincides with the number of positive eigenvalues of ℒ\mathcal{L} acting on ℝ\mathbb{R}, we can rely on the results of [BCJ+18, SS00]. We note that some results on point spectra of truncated operators include Sections 2.5 and 4 of [Dan08] and [KKL99].

Lemma 3.19.

Let 0≤λ1​(L)≤λ2​(L)≤⋯≤λn​(L)0\leq\lambda_{1}(L)\leq\lambda_{2}(L)\leq\dots\leq\lambda_{n}(L) be the non-negative eigenvalues for the operator ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L}. Each λj​(L)\lambda_{j}(L) is

  1. 1.

    a continuously varying function of LL;

  2. 2.

    strictly increasing with LL.

Proof.
  1. 1.

    Since the essential spectrum of ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} is strictly negative, the eigenvalues of ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} can be thought of as the eigenvalues of a continuous family of finite dimensional operators parameterized by LL. See for example, [Kat66][Section II.5] or [Dan08][Sections 2.5, 4].

  2. 2.

    The proof of this statement is virtually identical to that of [BCJ+18][Remark 3.5].

∎

Finally, we have that Theorem 3.1 can be extended to ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Theorem 3.20.

There exists L∞∈ℝL_{\infty}\in\mathbb{R} such that for all L>L∞L>L_{\infty} the number of positive eigenvalues of the restricted operator ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} (Equation 3.7) coincides with that of the operator ℒ\mathcal{L} on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Additionally, if we denote the number of positive eigenvalues of a differential operator ℋ\mathcal{H} as Mor​(ℋ)\text{Mor}(\mathcal{H}), then

  1. 1.

    LL is not a conjugate point and ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} is invertible;

  2. 2.

    the number of conjugate points of ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} is finite and independent of LL, meaning

    Mor​(ℒ)=#​ conjugate points in ​(−∞,+∞).\text{Mor}(\mathcal{L})=\#\text{ conjugate points in }(-\infty,+\infty).
Proof.

The argument relies on Lemma 3.19 and is virtually identical to [BCJ+18][Theorem 4.1]. ∎

4 Numerical Computation of Conjugate Points

Here, we describe how we numerically compute the conjugate points for three symmetric pulse solutions to the Swift-Hohenberg equation and compare the number of conjugate points to the number of unstable eigenvalues computed experimentally using Fourier spectral methods.

Recalling the vector field parameters ν\nu and μ\mu from (1.2), we consider two specific pairs of parameters (ν,μ)(\nu,\mu). In the first, we follow [BKL+09b, BK06], and set ν=1.6\nu=1.6 and μ=0.05\mu=0.05. These parameter values lie in the non-snaking region and there are two branches of symmetric pulse solutions. In the second set of parameter values, we set ν=1.6\nu=1.6 and μ=0.20\mu=0.20. This lies within an interesting parameter region in which the system displays homoclinic snaking. For these parameter values, there are infinitely many symmetric pulse solutions.

Using perturbation theory, it was shown in [BK06] that the two branches of the symmetric pulse solutions can be approximated via

uϕ(x;ν,μ)=22​μγsech(x​μ2)cos(x+ϕ),γ=38​ν29−3,ϕ=0,π.u_{\phi}(x;\nu,\mu)=2\sqrt{\frac{2\mu}{\gamma}}\text{sech}\left(\frac{x\sqrt{\mu}}{2}\right)\cos(x+\phi),\qquad\gamma=\frac{38\nu^{2}}{9}-3,\qquad\phi=0,\pi. (4.1)

We will refer to stationary symmetric pulse solutions to (1.1) as φϕ​(x,ν,μ)\varphi_{\phi}(x;\nu,\mu), where ϕ\phi denotes the phase condition from the approximation uϕu_{\phi}. It was found via numerical experiments that in the non-snaking region, the ϕ=π\phi=\pi branch has 22 unstable eigenvalues and the ϕ=0\phi=0 branch has 11 unstable eigenvalue [BK06]. We corroborate these findings and show that the pulse solution in the snaking region has 00 unstable eigenvalues and is therefore spectrally stable. We note that these computations of eigenvalue counts are not mathematical proofs as such, and in future work we plan validate this via computer-assisted proof; see Section 5 for more discussion.

4.1 Eigenvalues via Fourier Spectral Methods

We reproduce results found in [BK06] using spectral methods similar to those found in [ACLS08]. We will write the normal form approximation uϕu_{\phi} for a pulse solution on the interval from [−Lf,Lf][-L_{f},L_{f}] in its Fourier expansion, up to order NN, and formulate the accompanying system of ODEs. We can then perform Newton’s method to refine the Fourier coefficients to obtain a better approximation of the pulse solution.

We begin by writing the pulse in its Fourier expansion,

φ⁡(x)=∑k=−∞∞ak​ei​π​k​x/Lf.\varphi(x)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}a_{k}e^{i\pi kx/L_{f}}. (4.2)

Truncating this expansion at order NN gives the truncated approximation for the pulse solution

φ(N)​(x)=∑k=−NNak​ei​π​k​x/Lf.\varphi^{(N)}(x)=\sum_{k=-N}^{N}a_{k}e^{i\pi kx/L_{f}}. (4.3)

Define a=(a−N,…,aN)a=(a_{-N},\dots,a_{N}) to be the vector of Fourier coefficients. By plugging (4.3) into (1.1), we obtain the 2​N+12N+1 dimensional system of ODEs given by the operator F:ℝ2​N+1→ℝ2​N+1F:\mathbb{R}^{2N+1}\to\mathbb{R}^{2N+1}, whose zeros correspond to the Fourier coefficients of a solution to (1.1). For k=−N,…,Nk=-N,\dots,N, the kkth component of FF is given via

Fk​(a)=[−μ−(1−k2​π2Lf2)2]​ak−(a∗a∗a)k+ν​(a∗a)k.F_{k}(a)=\left[-\mu-\left(1-\frac{k^{2}\pi^{2}}{L_{f}^{2}}\right)^{2}\right]a_{k}-(a*a*a)_{k}+\nu(a*a)_{k}. (4.4)

The operation ∗* is defined by

(a∗a)k=∑k1+k2=kki∈ℤak1​ak2​ and ​(a∗a∗a)k=∑k1+k2+k3=kki∈ℤak1​ak2​ak3.(a*a)_{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k_{1}+k_{2}=k\\ k_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}a_{k_{1}}a_{k_{2}}\ \text{ and }(a*a*a)_{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}=k\\ k_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}a_{k_{1}}a_{k_{2}}a_{k_{3}}.

Our goal is to use the Fourier coefficients of uϕu_{\phi} as the initial condition and run Newton’s method on F⁡(a)F(a) to obtain an approximation of the NNth order truncated pulse solution φϕ(N)​(x)\varphi^{(N)}_{\phi}(x). However, due to translational symmetry, D​F​(a)DF(a) has a zero eigenvalue, so we cannot compute Newton’s method on the Fourier coefficients for the entire pulse profile on [−Lf,Lf][-L_{f},L_{f}]. To get around this, we perform Newton’s method on half of the pulse profile on [0,Lf][0,L_{f}] and refine the coefficients (a0,…,aN)(a_{0},\dots,a_{N}). Therefore, when performing Newton’s method, we use an N+1N+1 dimensional system of ODEs with the kkth component given by (4.4) for k=0,…,N+1k=0,\dots,N+1. Finally, since φ\varphi is symmetric, it is the case that ak=a−ka_{k}=a_{-k}, which allows us to recover the approximation for the entire pulse.

By using the Fourier coefficients of uϕ​(x)u_{\phi}(x) as the initial condition, we can run Newton’s method to obtain the approximation of the NNth order truncated pulse solution φϕ(N)​(x)\varphi^{(N)}_{\phi}(x) on the interval [−Lf,Lf]=[−100,100][-L_{f},L_{f}]=[-100,100]. We refer to the numerical approximation of the truncated pulse solution as φ¯ϕ(N)​(x)\bar{\varphi}^{(N)}_{\phi}(x). The approximations are given in Figure 10(b). We note that for μ=0.2\mu=0.2, we are far from the regime where the normal form gives a good approximation, and we use 3​uϕ​(x)3u_{\phi}(x) as the initial seed for Newton’s method.

Denote the vector of approximate Fourier coefficients obtained via Newton’s method for a pulse solution as a¯\bar{a}. One can estimate the spectrum of the associated pulse solution by computing the eigenvalues of the matrix D​F​(a¯)DF(\bar{a}). The eigenvalues for our example pulse solutions are given in Table 2. For the parameters ν=1.6\nu=1.6 and μ=0.05\mu=0.05, these results are consistent with the results found in [BK06].

4.2 Eigenvalues via Conjugate Points

We now compute the number of conjugate points for the two symmetric pulse solutions. We have shown there exists L+>0L_{+}>0 such that the conjugate points are all contained in the interval (−∞,L+](-\infty,L_{+}]. In this work, our numerics serve as a proof-of-concept, so it is sufficient to choose Lc​pL_{cp} large via experimentation and compute the conjugate points on the interval from [−Lc​p,Lc​p][-L_{cp},L_{cp}].

In order to compute numerical approximations for the conjugate points associated to each pulse solution, we must first approximate the unstable subspace, 𝔼−u,ϕ​(x,0)\mathbb{E}^{u,\phi}_{-}(x;0) on the interval from [−L,L][-L,L]. The basis vectors for 𝔼−u,ϕ​(x,0)\mathbb{E}^{u,\phi}_{-}(x;0) solve the nonautonomous system given by (1.8). We treat this as an autonomous problem by simultaneously computing the pulse φ\varphi so that we can use ode45 in Matlab to integrate. After computing an approximation for the unstable subspace, we can use the following result to detect conjugate points.

Lemma 4.1.

Denote the frame matrix of 𝔼−u​(x,0)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x;0) as

(M1​(x)M2​(x)M3​(x)),M1​(x),M3​(x)∈ℝ1×2,M2​(x)∈ℝ2×2\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{2}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix},\qquad M_{1}(x),M_{3}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 2},M_{2}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}

and recall the reference plane ℓ∗s​a​n​d\ell_{*}^{sand} given in Definition 3.4. Then 𝔼−u​(x,0)∩ℓ∗s​a​n​d≠{0}\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x;0)\cap\ell_{*}^{sand}\neq\{0\} if and only if det(M1​(x)M3​(x))=0\det\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix}=0.

Proof.

First, suppose that 𝔼−u​(x)∩ℓ∗s​a​n​d≠{0}\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x)\cap\ell_{*}^{sand}\neq\{0\}. Then by definition, there is a nonzero vector v=(v1,v2)v=(v_{1},v_{2}) such that

(M1​(x)M2​(x)M3​(x))​(v1v2)=(0v~2v~30),v~2,v~3∈ℝ.\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{2}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}v_{1}\\ v_{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \tilde{v}_{2}\\ \tilde{v}_{3}\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\qquad\tilde{v}_{2},\tilde{v}_{3}\in\mathbb{R}.

However, this means (M1​(x)M3​(x))​v=0\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix}v=0. Thus, ker⁡(M1​(x)M3​(x))\ker\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix} is nontrivial so det(M1​(x)M3​(x))=0\det\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix}=0.

Now suppose that det(M1​(x)M3​(x))=0\det\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix}=0. Then there is a vector vv such that (M1​(x)M3​(x))​v=0\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix}v=0. Since 𝔼−u​(x)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x) is a Lagrangian subspace, its frame matrix has full rank, so

(M1​(x)M2​(x)M3​(x))​(v1v2)=(0v~2v~30),\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}(x)\\ M_{2}(x)\\ M_{3}(x)\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}v_{1}\\ v_{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \tilde{v}_{2}\\ \tilde{v}_{3}\\ 0\end{pmatrix},

with at least one of v~2,v~3\tilde{v}_{2},\tilde{v}_{3} nonzero. Therefore, there is a nonzero vector in the intersection of 𝔼−u​(x)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x) and ℓ∗s​a​n​d\ell_{*}^{sand}. ∎

Remark 4.2.

We note that, since we fully compute the frame for the unstable subspace, we could use this frame to determine the spectral flow associated with this path of Lagrangian frames [Fur04]. This would allow us to generalize our method to instances where monotonicity is not guaranteed. However, since we have shown the crossings are monotonic, we do not need to take this approach here.

Thus, we calculate the determinant of the submatrix formed from the first and fourth rows of the frame matrix for 𝔼−u,ϕ​(x,0)\mathbb{E}^{u,\phi}_{-}(x;0), calculate the zeros corresponding to conjugate points. We fix Lc​p=60L_{cp}=60 and compute

𝔼−u,ϕ​(x,0)=(||W1−,uW2−,u||).\mathbb{E}^{u,\phi}_{-}(x;0)=\begin{pmatrix}|&|\\ W^{-,u}_{1}&W^{-,u}_{2}\\ |&|\end{pmatrix}.

Define

detA⁡(x)=det((W1−,u)1(W2−,u)1(W1−,u)4(W2−,u)4).\det A(x)=\det\begin{pmatrix}(W^{-,u}_{1})_{1}&(W^{-,u}_{2})_{1}\\ (W^{-,u}_{1})_{4}&(W^{-,u}_{2})_{4}\end{pmatrix}.

Via Lemma 4.1, the zeros of detA⁡(x)\det A(x) correspond to conjugate points. To verify that each of the conjugate points correspond to a simple crossing, we check that ∥A(x∗))∥>10−3\|A(x_{*}))\|>10^{-3} at each of the conjugate points x∗x_{*}.

First, we look at the pulse solution with parameter values ν=1.6\nu=1.6, μ=0.05\mu=0.05 and phase condition ϕ=0\phi=0. This solution lies outside of the snaking region and we denote it via φ0​(x,1.6,0.05)\varphi_{0}(x;1.6,0.05). Via Fourier methods, we find one unstable eigenvalue (Figure 11(b)). When plotting the determinant of A⁡(x)A(x) associated to this pulse, we see that there is one zero (Figure 11(c)).

Second, we look at the other symmetric pulse with parameter values ν=1.6\nu=1.6 and μ=0.05\mu=0.05 with phase condition ϕ=π\phi=\pi. We denote this pulse as φπ​(x,1.6,0.05)\varphi_{\pi}(x;1.6,0.05). Via Fourier spectral methods, we find two unstable eigenvalues (Figure 12(b)). By inspecting the plot of detA⁡(x)\det A(x), we see that there are two zeros (Figure 12(c)).

Taken together, the information about φϕ​(x,1.6,0.05)\varphi_{\phi}(x;1.6,0.05), with ϕ=0,π\phi=0,\pi contained in Figures 11 and 12 are consistent with results found in [BK06] and allow us to conclude that these two pulses are spectrally unstable. Since spectral stability in this case is necessary for linear and nonlinear stability, we see that these two pulses are linear/nonlinearly unstable as well.

Finally, we consider the symmetric pulse with parameter values ν=1.6\nu=1.6, μ=.20\mu=.20 and phase condition ϕ=0\phi=0. This pulse lies within the parameter region that supports homoclinic snaking and is one of infinitely many asymmetric pulses for these parameter values. By performing Fourier spectral methods, we find no unstable eigenvalues. Additionally, when we plot detA⁡(x)\det A(x), we see that there are no zeros. This information can be found in Figure 13.

Remark 4.3.

The behavior at the tails of these plots are determined by the asymptotic coefficient matrix B∞B_{\infty} given in (1.12). Since B∞B_{\infty} has complex conjugate eigenvalues, we observe periodic behavior. Indeed, the trajectory 𝔼−u​(x)\mathbb{E}_{-}^{u}(x) may be seen to be be a heteroclinic orbit within the space of Grassmanians, limiting to the point 𝔼−u​(−∞)\mathbb{E}_{-}^{u}(-\infty) as x→−∞x\to-\infty, and limiting to a periodic orbit as x→+∞x\to+\infty.

Another visualization of intersections between the unstable subspace and the sandwich plane can be done via the Plücker coordinates. Given two vectors in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, v1=∑j=14aj​ejv_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{4}a_{j}e_{j} and v2=∑j=14bj​ejv_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{4}b_{j}e_{j}, the wedge product v1∧v2v_{1}\wedge v_{2} is given by

v1∧v2=∑1≤i<j≤4(ai​bj−aj​bi)​(ei∧ej).v_{1}\wedge v_{2}=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 4}(a_{i}b_{j}-a_{j}b_{i})(e_{i}\wedge e_{j}).

The wedge product defines an alternating tensor product of vectors (i.e. ei∧ej=−ej∧eie_{i}\wedge e_{j}=-e_{j}\wedge e_{i}) and the kt​hk^{th} exterior product of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is commonly denoted by ⋀k(ℝn)\bigwedge^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and has dimension (nk)n\choose k.

One defines the Plücker embedding of a Grassmannian by identifying the vectors spanning a subspace with their projectivized wedge product. For the case of, say, 2-dimensional subspaces of ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, that is

s​p​a​n​{v1,v2}↦[v1∧v2]span\{v_{1},v_{2}\}\mapsto[v_{1}\wedge v_{2}]

where [v1∧v2][v_{1}\wedge v_{2}] denotes the equivalence class α⁡(v1∧v2)\alpha(v_{1}\wedge v_{2}) for all α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.

Definition 4.4.

Consider the 2-dimensional subspace W⊆ℝ4W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{4} spanned by the vectors v1=∑j=14aj​ejv_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{4}a_{j}e_{j} and v2=∑j=14bj​ejv_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{4}b_{j}e_{j}. Given the vectors v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}, for all 1≤i<j≤41\leq i<j\leq 4 we define their unnormalized Plücker coordinate P~i​j\tilde{P}_{ij}, and their normalized Plücker coordinates Pi​jP_{ij} as:

P~i​j\displaystyle\tilde{P}_{ij} =ai​bj−aj​bi,\displaystyle=a_{i}b_{j}-a_{j}b_{i}, Pi​j\displaystyle P_{ij} =P~i​j‖P~‖.\displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{P}_{ij}}{\|\tilde{P}\|}. (4.5)

where ‖P~‖2=∑1≤i<j≤4P~i​j2\|\tilde{P}\|^{2}=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 4}\tilde{P}_{ij}^{2}.

Note that if {v1,v2}\{v_{1},v_{2}\} and {w1,w2}\{w_{1},w_{2}\} span the same subspace and have Plücker coordinates Pi​jP_{ij} and Qi​jQ_{ij} respectively, then either Pi​j=Qi​jP_{ij}=Q_{ij} or Pi​j=−Qi​jP_{ij}=-Q_{ij} for all 1≤i<j≤41\leq i<j\leq 4.

The Plücker coordinates provides us with a convenient coordinate system to plot the trajectory of 𝔼−u​(x)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x) through Λ⁡(2)\Lambda(2) for the three pulse solutions we have considered thus far. Note that the Lagrangian Grassmannian Λ⁡(2)\Lambda(2) is 3 dimensional and ⋀2(ℝ4)\bigwedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{4}) is 6 dimensional, so some amount of information will be discarded [Lee03]. In Figures 15 and 17 we plot the first three Plücker coordinates P12,P13,P14P_{12},P_{13},P_{14} of the trajectory of 𝔼−u​(x)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x).

To depict the train of ℓ∗s​a​n​d\ell_{*}^{sand}, suppose that ℓ∩ℓ∗s​a​n​d≠{0}\ell\cap\ell_{*}^{sand}\neq\{0\} and ℓ=s​p​a​n​{v1,v2}\ell=span\{v_{1},v_{2}\} with v1∈ℓ∗s​a​n​dv_{1}\in\ell_{*}^{sand}. Without loss of generality (due to the Lagrangian property) we may write

5 Future Directions

In this work, we have shown that the number of unstable eigenvalues of pulse solutions to the Swift-Hohenberg equation corresponds to the number of conjugate points, as long as Hypothesis 3.17 holds. Additionally, we have derived a novel numerical method for computing the stability of these solutions. However, the computations in Section 4 do not provide a mathematical proof of the spectral stability of pulse solutions. We are currently developing a method using validated numerics to do so, similar to that done in [BJ22]. In order to construct a computer assisted proof of the stability of a given solution φ\varphi, we must:

  1. 1.

    Compute a numerical approximation of φ\varphi with error bounds;

  2. 2.

    determine the interval [−L−,L+][-L_{-},L_{+}] on which the conjugate points occur;

  3. 3.

    approximate 𝔼−u​(−L−,0)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(-L_{-};0) and integrate forward to 𝔼−u​(L+,0)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(L_{+};0), with rigorous error bounds;

  4. 4.

    count the number of times 𝔼−u​(x,0)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x;0) intersects ℓ∗s​a​n​d\ell_{*}^{sand} for x∈[−L−,L+]x\in[-L_{-},L_{+}], and show that each intersection is 1 dimensional.

Computing 𝔼−u​(x,0)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x;0) on this interval is complicated by the presence of a so-called external resonance in the spatial eigenvalues. This resonance was also presence in the work of [BJ22], but the computer assisted proof in this work considered lower order approximations, so this was not an issue. We seek a higher order approximation of the subspace 𝔼−u​(x,0)\mathbb{E}^{u}_{-}(x;0) and so we must address this resonance.

It would be very interesting to try to remove the need for Hypothesis 3.17. This could be done in one of two ways. First, one could attempt to prove that this hypothesis in fact always holds for solutions of the Swift-Hohenberg equation. Our numerics for the example pulses that we consider here suggests that this might indeed be true. Additionally, one could also seek to extend the results from §2.2 to situations in which, at a degenerate crossing, the entire crossing form need not be degenerate. We suspect that proving such results should be possible, and indeed this would be an interesting direction to pursue, even if it were to turn out that, for Swift-Hohenberg, Hypothesis 3.17 did always hold, since this might not be the case for other PDEs.

Additionally, the use of higher order crossing forms could be used to prove a result relating the number of conjugate points to the number of unstable eigenvalues of the fourth order Hamiltonian system

ut=−∂x4u−P∂x2u−u+u2u_{t}=-\partial_{x}^{4}u-P\partial_{x}^{2}u-u+u^{2} (5.1)

where PP is a real parameter. In a certain parameter region, this system admits stationary localized solutions, which are studied in [Buf95, BCT96]. In [BCT96], these pulse solutions are classified via a sequence of integers n⁡(ℓ1,…,ℓn−1)n(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{n-1}), called the BCT classification, where nn is the number of major local extrema and ℓi\ell_{i} are related to the number of zeros between the major local extrema. Numerical experiments suggest that the number of conjugate points associated to these solutions can be computed via the information encoded in the BCT classification [TJBD09]. If this were to be proved rigorously, this result could be viewed as an extension of Sturm-Liouville theory to fourth order systems. Rigorously justifying the results of [TJBD09] will be the subject of future work.

A.2 An Explicit Example with the Maslov Index

Here we present an explicit example using a path of Lagrangian subspaces whose basis vectors are constructed from solutions to an ODE. We compute the Maslov index with respect to the sandwich plane using the crossing form. This example serves two purposes. The first is to illustrate the subtlety in expressing a path of Lagrangian subspaces as a graph that is discussed in Remark 3.12. The second is to concretely show the relationship between the higher order crossing forms and the derivatives of the eigenvalues of the graph matrix (see Section 2.3).
